title: 3 Indian animals that plant forests

scenes.headline: Drop seeds up to 11–13 km away.
scenes.body: Tagged great and wreathed hornbills in Pakke Tiger Reserve, Arunachal, scattered seeds far from the parent tree.

scenes.headline: The elephant apple's best friend.
scenes.body: In Buxa, its seeds were 26.5× likelier to pass intact through an elephant than through cattle.

scenes.headline: Not just termites: fruit too.
scenes.body: Fruit showed up in 83% of dry-season scats in South India, and some seeds sprouted faster after the trip.

scenes.headline: Lose these animals, and big-seeded trees lose their gardeners.

caption:
Hornbills, elephants and sloth bears all move seeds for India's forests.

Elephant-apple seeds from elephant dung were also 1.5 times more likely to germinate than seeds from cattle dung.

Sources: Naniwadekar et al. (2019) Acta Oecologica; Sekar, Lee & Sukumar (2015) Ecology 96:2093; Sreekumar & Balakrishnan (2002) Biotropica. Footage: oriental pied hornbill; photo: Indian grey hornbill. Photos/video: Wikimedia Commons (credits on screen).
notes: Every list item is an Indian field study with its own number; reframes charismatic animals as forest builders.
